issues.description: The manuscript gives two incompatible operational definitions of the focal construct. One sentence defines moral incongruence as moral disapproval interacting with "severity of consequences," but the very next sentence redefines it as moral disapproval interacting with "frequency of use." This is not a trivial wording issue because the confirmatory analyses, measures, and theoretical claims depend on which construct is actually being tested.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

issues.description: The methods contradict themselves on whether problem-use measures are administered only to past-year users or to all respondents. This ambiguity changes the analytic sample, missingness pattern, and interpretation of zero scores, and it is central to reproducibility.
issues.quote:
Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.description: The same frequency measures are described with incompatible codings across sections. In the methods, pornography and gambling frequency are coded 1-6; in the supplemental materials the same scales are coded 0-5. This affects centering, inclusion thresholds, interaction terms, and reproducibility.
issues.quote:
participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

| Never (0) | Once or Twice (1) | Monthly (2) | Weekly (3) | Daily or Almost Daily (4) | More than Once Per Day (5)

issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen is described with incompatible response codings. The methods say responses range from 0 to 2, but the supplemental instrument uses 0, 2, and 4. This changes the total score metric and any cutoffs or effect sizes derived from it.
issues.quote:
Participants will respond to the prompt... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often).

| Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index appears to be miscoded. The methods describe the validated 0-3 response metric, but the supplemental instrument uses 0, 2, 4, and 5. This is not a harmless rescaling: it is nonlinear, departs from the validated scoring, and would invalidate comparability and interpretation.
issues.quote:
This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always).

| Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.description: The study relies heavily on a substantially modified ASSIST/NIDA screen, including altered alcohol wording, collapsed nicotine products, added cannabis, added gambling and pornography, and a changed response scale. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges that some of these uses are not validated. Because these modified measures are central outcomes, construct validity and comparability are compromised.
issues.quote: We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography... In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen provides a response range of Never to Daily or Almost Daily. For our use case... we will modify response options by adding an additional frequency category of more than once per day

issues.description: The ASSIST-derived composite averages items with different response ranges and different temporal reference periods. Three items use a 0-5 scale for the past 3 months, whereas two items use a 0/3/6 scale and ask about ever vs. past 3 months. Averaging these raw responses gives disproportionate weight to the 0/3/6 items and creates an arbitrary outcome metric with no stated validation.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.description: Key variables use incompatible time windows: behavior frequency is measured over the past 12 months, ASSIST problem items over the past 3 months or ever, the BPS over the last 6 months, and the PGSI over the last 12 months. This undermines interpretation of interactions and weakens cross-domain comparisons because predictors and outcomes are not aligned temporally.
issues.quote:
participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months...

“In the past three months, how often...”

“Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern...”

“In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you...”

“Thinking about the last 12 months...”

issues.description: The central moderator is assessed with single-item moral disapproval questions across all domains. Single-item measures provide limited reliability and may attenuate interactions unevenly across behaviors, making apparent domain differences difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Additionally, we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions... For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong”

issues.description: The manuscript equates moral incongruence with a statistical interaction between frequency and disapproval. But a multiplicative interaction is not the same thing as an individual-level discrepancy between behavior and values, and simple frequency is not a direct measure of dysregulation. This operationalization risks testing a statistical artifact rather than the construct named in the theory.
issues.quote: That is, we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior) influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.description: Several outcome measures include guilt or self-evaluative items that overlap conceptually with the predictor of moral disapproval. This content overlap can mechanically inflate associations between moral disapproval and reported "addiction" or "problems," making it difficult to separate morality from symptom reporting.
issues.quote:
5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly claims to study "self-perceived feelings of addiction," but the planned outcomes are heterogeneous symptom/problem scales (PGSI, BPS, modified ASSIST items) rather than a common direct self-identification measure. This is a construct mismatch, especially when drawing conclusions about self-perceived addiction across domains.
issues.quote:
we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction to both behaviors...

problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index...

self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen

issues.description: The central cross-domain claim depends on comparing interaction effects across behaviors, but the outcomes are measured with different instruments that differ in content, reliability, scaling, and timeframe. Apparent uniqueness for pornography could therefore reflect measurement differences rather than a true substantive difference.
issues.quote:
with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively).

Table 1
Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.description: The manuscript uses causal language (e.g., "influences") for a cross-sectional, same-source survey design. Even the authors acknowledge that the data are cross-sectional and cannot establish temporal ordering. The design can test associations, not whether moral incongruence influences addiction feelings.
issues.quote:
we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

This sample is cross-sectional, which limits the temporal ordering of variables.

issues.description: The manuscript proposes to use cross-sectional survey interactions as evidence for the validity of a diagnostic caveat in ICD-11 and as evidence that addiction self-reports are systematically biased by morality. These are much stronger claims than the design can support; neither diagnostic validity nor measurement bias can be established from these analyses alone.
issues.quote:
should we find that moral incongruence... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI... there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

should we find that moral incongruence predicts self-reported addiction or dysregulation for more than just pornography use... it would suggest that community and population-based research using self-reported symptoms of addiction might be systematically biased by participant morality.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the sample as nationally representative, but the sampling description only states that YouGov respondents are matched to norms. Without a probability design or explicit weighting plan, calling the resulting pooled sample "nationally representative" is too strong.
issues.quote:
Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population

issues.description: The design adds a large oversample of recent sports bettors, but the analysis plan does not explain whether models will be weighted, stratified, or adjusted for this nonrepresentative enrichment. Pooling these respondents could distort associations for gambling and potentially other addictive behaviors as well.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: Because the study uses a matched panel plus a behavior-specific oversample, the manuscript needs a clear plan for survey weights, design effects, and whether inferential models will be weighted. None is provided, which makes the representativeness and even the target estimand unclear.
issues.quote:
Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.description: The equivalence margin is internally inconsistent. The plan first states a SESOI of δ = .27, then immediately says the SESOI is based on β = .11, and later refers to an equivalence region of |.11|. The confirmatory test cannot be evaluated when the null region itself is contradictory.
issues.quote:
We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

Given this variability, we elected to set our SESOI (δ) ... equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11...

Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.description: The authors plan to redefine the equivalence region based on the observed pornography effect if initial results are contrary to hypotheses. This is a result-contingent, data-dependent decision that undermines the confirmatory status of the equivalence test and increases interpretive flexibility.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.description: The analytic plan is inconsistent about whether interaction terms are computed from centered variables or from raw variables. This matters for interpretability, multicollinearity, and reproducibility of the registered analysis.
issues.quote:
focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated.

For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.description: The plan says supplemental analyses will be run if assumptions are "substantially violated," but it does not define thresholds for violation or specify which alternative models will be used. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom in a registered report.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.description: The equivalence margin is described in terms of standardized betas from prior work, but the regression plan describes using raw variables and does not clearly explain how standardized interaction coefficients and their confidence intervals will be obtained for the confirmatory test. This makes the primary hypothesis test poorly specified.
issues.quote:
For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction... fall fully within our equivalence region

issues.description: The manuscript alternates among seven behaviors, eight moderation analyses, and multiple outcomes for pornography and gambling. Table 1 lists both validated scales and modified ASSIST outcomes for pornography and gambling, but the text later says there will be only eight moderation analyses using the validated measures. The confirmatory outcome set is therefore not fully specified.
issues.quote:
Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.

In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses...

Table 1
Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items
Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.description: Gambling frequency is first described as a single-item measure, but then the manuscript says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplement also shows only one gambling-frequency item. This contradiction leaves the actual predictor unspecified.
issues.quote:
We will assess gambling frequency using a single item.

To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between treating tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine as separate outcomes and as a single combined tobacco/nicotine item. This affects the number of analyses, variable construction, and interpretation of results for nicotine-related behaviors.
issues.quote:
Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

Tobacco or nicotine products, including cigarettes and smoked tobacco, as well as smokeless tobacco and non-cigarette nicotine products (vape/e-cig products)

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that key equivalence tests for rare behaviors are likely underpowered, with achieved power as low as .301 for prescription drug misuse. Underpowered equivalence tests are particularly problematic because failure to reject nonequivalence does not support the intended null-like inference.
issues.quote:
it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small (See Table 2).

Prescription Drug Misuse | Effective N 140 | Smallest Detectable Effect Size f2 .057 | Estimated Achieved power for f2= .015 | .301

issues.description: The plan assumes away missing data in a sensitive survey about pornography, gambling, and substance use. That is unrealistic, and no strategy is given for item nonresponse, partial completes, or respondents who skip stigma-laden items. This threatens reproducibility and may bias results.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.description: The authors note that analyses will use different subsets of the sample, but do not specify the exact inclusion rules for each model, whether nonusers are retained with zero outcomes, or how respondents who were not administered gated items will be handled. This prevents full evaluation or replication of the confirmatory analyses.
issues.quote: Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.description: The manuscript specifies eight moderation analyses and several direct-effect tests, but only mentions Holm adjustment for exploratory bivariate correlations. No multiplicity strategy is specified for the primary confirmatory hypotheses, which raises the risk of inflated false-positive inference.
issues.quote:
Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics...

In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses

issues.description: The pornography-frequency item only captures solitary viewing. Conclusions are nevertheless framed as applying to pornography use broadly. This excludes partnered use and narrows the construct relative to the claims made in the paper.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.description: Gender is entered as a binary covariate coded male vs. not-male. This collapses women and nonbinary respondents into a single residual category and is an imprecise operationalization of gender for a study on morality and sexuality-related behaviors.
issues.quote: with gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome.

issues.description: The study replaces the validated heavy-drinking threshold item with a general alcohol-frequency question. This changes the construct from risk-relevant heavy use to any alcohol use, reducing comparability with the original screen and potentially weakening interpretation of alcohol-related moral incongruence.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.description: The primary models use ordinary least squares despite bounded, ordinal, and likely zero-inflated outcome variables (e.g., BPS sums, PGSI responses, ASSIST composites), especially for low-prevalence substances. The plan does not pre-specify more appropriate generalized models, so coefficient estimates and standard errors may be distorted.
issues.quote:
we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software...

Although Ordinary Least Squares techniques ... in large sample sizes are often robust against some violations

issues.description: The paper makes strong cross-behavior claims while planning to adjust only for age, gender, and religiousness, despite having other relevant panel variables available (e.g., ideology, state, income). For substances and gambling, legal context and social norms plausibly affect both moral disapproval and self-reported problems, so the comparative claims remain vulnerable to omitted-variable confounding.
issues.quote:
In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates...

YouGov Panel Data Included
...
State of Residence
...
Ideology
...
Family income

issues.description: The supplemental alcohol item for men appears to contain a wording error: the prompt refers to more than 5 drinks, but the response row is labeled "More than four drinks." Even if not central to the primary analysis, this indicates a lack of survey specification precision.
issues.quote:
IF GENDER = MAN

In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?

More than four drinks (1)
